To accomplish this work, we employ NREL’s System Advisor Model (SAM) new ETES modeling capability to evaluate the impact of introducing PCM particles into the 3rd generation molten salts (i.e., 45.98% MgCl2, 38.91% KCl, 15.11% NaCl). However, to complete this work, we were required to modify SAM’s ETES model to (i) capture the impact of latent heat behavior within a TES medium and (ii) enable the use of sCO power cycle predicted performance from 2 an external Python model. 1.2 PCMs Latent Heat The thermodynamic modeling within SAM’s ETES model uses energy balances to evaluate heat and power flows into and out of the system over time. Specifically, the model uses the approximate form for the change of enthalpy, i.e., the product of specific heat and change in temperature. Before this project, SAM’s ETES model evaluated specific heat at the midpoint of a temperature range to characterize energy flows. The midpoint temperature specific heat approximation is appropriate for fluids with a linear relationship between specific heat and temperature, i.e., molten salts. However, this approach breaks down when the relationship between specific heat and temperature is non-linear, i.e., phase change occurs or large temperature changes. To address this, we updated the ETES model to evaluate the average specific heat using numerical integration over the process temperature range, equation (1). 1 𝑇𝑓 ̅𝐶̅̅ = ∫ 𝐶 (𝑇)𝑑𝑇 (1) 𝑝 𝑇 −𝑇 𝑝 𝑓 𝑖 𝑇𝑖 Where 𝐶̅̅̅ is the average specific heat, 𝑇 is the final temperature, 𝑇 is the initial temperature, 𝑝 𝑓 𝑖 and 𝐶 (𝑇) is the specific heat as a function of temperature. By calculating the specific heat of the 𝑝 process using numerical integration rather than at the midpoint temperature, we enabled SAM’s ETES model to capture non-linear specific heat and temperature relationships that occur during the phase change process. 1.3 sCO Cycle 2 For this work, the ETES system used a sCO power cycle as the discharge heat engine. Due to 2 the immaturity of sCO power cycles, SAM does not provide a default model to estimate sCO 2 2 cycle performance for annual simulations, i.e., of the ETES model. Instead, SAM provides a standardized format for importing a user-defined power cycle performance as a function of heat input, hot TES temperature, and ambient temperature. Previous work at NREL developed a design point and off-design performance models for sCO power cycles (Neises et al. 2014, 2 Neises et al. 2019), which can be called from Python. Additionally, previous work created an sCO cycle integration macro within SAM that enables users to import results from the Python 2 sCO cycle model directly into SAM’s user-defined power cycle. Before this work, this macro 2 was only available within SAM’s molten salt power tower concentrating solar power model. As a part of this work, we enabled the sCO cycle integration macro to be used for SAM’s ETES 2 model. This allows us to predict the sCO cycle performance using various PCM salt slurries and 2 import that performance directly into SAM to estimate the system’s annual performance. 9 This report
